posts.author: Miggmaru
posts.body:
This is something I think about a lot. I want to make things because I have stories I need to tell, or I feel like I'll die. I want to make stories that bring joy to people and comfort them or make them think. People need art. I need art. I want to give that to them.
Why do you create? Why do you want to make games?

posts.author: TotalyNate
posts.body:
Well... I make jrpgs because they have always been apart of my life. I've always loved them. I would watch my dad play final fantasy before I could even read.
Something about creating a world, your OWN world, especially in a way that is extremely nostalgic and historical for me, is just so satisfying.
My love for these kind of games and the joy they have brought, and still bring me, that's why I make games.

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body: Video games are the most accessible medium for me to share my storywriting and I've always wanted to iterate on game design I've liked by adding tweaks or making up new scenarios by mixing techniques from different games (sometimes even entirely different genres) together.

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
I've always liked to make things. Writing, drawing, sewing, set design, I've always loved it all. My gaming experiences as a kid were very limited, I was never allowed a console and my PC games were all edu-tainment reading games. I discovered RPGs by way of Aveyond, an RPG Maker game, when I was in eighth grade and experienced a quantum shift in my understanding of what games were. What do you mean games are art + story? How did I never know this? This sounds fantastic!
And it is! It's the ability to do all my favorite things in one place. Not only can I tell a story, I can tell multiple stories that braid together later on! Not only can I describe an interesting place, I can show it to you! You can walk around the magic castle, the little village in the mountains, the murder mystery mansion. You can have the thrill of finding the secret passage yourself, rather than having me tell you about it in narration.
And something I really like about RPG Maker in particular is that the graphics aren't so detailed that there isn't room for imagination. One of the things that captivated me so much about Aveyond (and still does) and indeed the RMXP RTP style on the whole is how much detail the sprites and tiles have, but how much room remains is to fill in details yourself. This blue robe the little pixel-bean is wearing--what details should it have in his portrait art? This spell animation--how could I elaborate on that for cover art?
It's a fantastic blend of my favorite creative outlets. I get to write, draw, and dress sets all at the same time! What's not to love? If someone else loves my work, all the better--but first and foremost, I do this for me.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body: I want to make games that I want to play. If anyone else ever plays one of my games, that is a bonus (particularly if they enjoy it). I like aspects of games that I suspect are not the choices of the majority. For instance, I prefer the front-view battle system, like random encounters when set-up carefully, and want to choose the party so that repeat play-thoughs feel different.

Well, I just like to create. That's the main driver

posts.author: Indinera
posts.body:
For the hot girls and the $$$.
No seriously, it's not
only
for that lol
I love creating because it's stimulating, exciting and a lot of fun, it's one of the very best activities one can have in my opinion. I would consider it time well spent, and food for the mind.
In the case of games specifically, I particularly like imagining characters, telling stories, adding secrets, and then see players try to find them or react to the twists and climaxes in my stories, or the personalities of my characters. It's a great feeling and it helps you to develop and give the best of yourself.
So the creation itself is fun, and the interaction with the community is also fun.

posts.author: Artille
posts.body:
I like it because it feels like putting puzzles together.
It's exciting to discover new mechanics, be inspired by different things, recreate old ideas and adapt them to your own, and overall just
learn
.
It's also a nice way of thinking outside the box — working on a completely different scale and medium than usual, with its own challenges and rewards.
And of course, it's also about expressing my own thoughts and bringing a smile to people’s faces, whether they discover a "real" hidden secret (old-school style) or dive into the depth of the lore.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Because I enjoy it. At my age, I've finally learned that time is precious and you should strive to do those things that you enjoy. If you don't enjoy something and it isn't necessary for your survival in the regular adult world (short or long term), it might not be worth your time.
Also, I've always wanted to make my own game that, like
@Piyan Glupak
, I would enjoy playing. For game developing and writing, I have a primary audience of one.
There are three factors that drive my game developing right now.
Am I enjoying what I'm doing?
Is this something that I'd enjoy playing?
Does this satisfy my curiosity of "can I do this"?
Many of my game making experiments come directly from that last question. I wonder if I can...?
I also have been writing for over 40 years. Because I enjoy it. I have always told myself stories to pass the time. Before I even started writing them down. Stories that interest me and entertain me. Some could call them day dreaming, but much more involved. My stories are for me.
So, with writing and game developing, I create for myself because I enjoy it. When I stop enjoying it, I'll stop doing it.
If anyone else appreciates what I have created, that is just an added bonus.
When I was much younger, first starting on my writing journey, I had fantasies of becoming rich, famous, and being celebrated as a great writer. But over the years, I came to appreciate that no matter how much success you end up having in any creative endeavor, if you enjoy what you do, you have already won. The return on your investment is a joy-filled, fulling life that you can look back on with satisfaction.
TLDR: See first sentence.

posts.author: Metzin
posts.body:
In my mind, I see a dreamy version of a world I wish I lived in--I want it to materialize in front of me because I can't quite see it fully.
I start building it, refining it--one bit at a time--filling in the gaps my mind doesn't see. And in the process, I uncover hidden parts that I didn't realize needed to be there.
Filling in the gaps is a welcome challenge of problem-solving, like a game in and of itself. But there are infinite possibilities, so it's always a delightful surprise to see what happens!
Being able to share what I built is a big part of the payoff, too!

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
For me, creation is a deeply spiritual act.  It is reaching into the ether to pull something into existence.  Stephen King coined it as "The voice of Gan".  It's a phrase that makes sense to me.
I create, because the creative force within me demands it be done.  The characters demand their stories be told.
Or, my soul yearns to find the freedom that my body cannot.
Creation for me is seldom a "conscious act".  I rarely decide "this is what the characters do, and why it makes sense".  It is most often "This is the event that happens" and then I listen to the characters for what they do and put it to page.  Or game engine.  Or whatever.
I'm just a conduit.  Just the messenger.  It's only my job to put what needs to be said and seen to compelling medium.

posts.author: TSR
posts.body:
Like most I create because I love to tell stories, create world and design rules and systems. As a kid I drew comic books and created board games; and I don't remember having ever played D&D as a player, always been the DM. So it was natural that I started making video games inspired by most classic rpgs of the 90's.
I've been doing it on & off for the last 30 years so I guess it kind of just became an habit
Never made much significant stuff over the years, but that doesn't matter, it's just a hobby and I'm far more interested in the process of making than the actual results.
Video games are a medium that best suits both sides of my personality: developing stories, drawing characters and monsters, creating maps, all of which stimulate my artistic side. But in the mean time, a video game is a computer program by nature for which programming is inherent. This in turn stimulates my more down-to-earth side. I like coding, but when I'm full of it, I can switch to other parts of game development and so on. This keeps my motivation on.​

posts.author: Krosis
posts.body:
Indinera said:
Why not? But it's a bit sad to pursue a creative endeavour just for it - especially an indie venture.
Click to expand...
I’m joking, of course, it’s not the only reason I’m making a game. By writing compelling stories and characters and exploring different aspects of their lives, I’ve learned a lot about my own. I truly enjoy immersing myself as a creator, and my values have changed a lot since I started following my passion.
I don’t even expect to make money. There’s an ongoing shift in entertainment right now, and while many people here look down on AI, the current engines are the worst they will ever be. Less than a decade from now, we’ll be drowning in entertainment. If someone’s only goal is to just throw a game into the world - just wait a while. But I'm not discouraged. If your goal is to explore yourself and learn more about life, then keep developing.
As Brandon Sanderson famously said:
“
You are the product, not your creations
.”
